meta.title: Who really said "If you want to fly, give up everything that weighs you down"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the Buddha. It is Toni Morrison's 'Song of Solomon' (1977) — Guitar Bains talking about a peacock — and the real line has a swear word in it, which is exactly the word the meme removed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you want to fly, give up everything that weighs you down'?
meta.ogDescription: A 1977 American novel, not a sutra. Toni Morrison wrote it, a character says it about a peacock, and the profanity was cut to make it pass as scripture.

answer.label: Toni Morrison — and the real wording is blunter
answer.authorDates: 1931–2019 · American novelist, editor and Nobel laureate
answer.sourceLine: It comes from Song of Solomon (1977), Toni Morrison’s third novel. Guitar Bains is explaining to Milkman why a peacock cannot get airborne — too much tail, too much jewellery, too much vanity — and finishes: ‘Can’t nobody fly with all that shit.’ The tidy inspirational version is that speech with the swearing taken out and the peacock deleted. Morrison died in 2019, so this is a copyrighted novel, not scripture.

docMeta.dd: Chapter 8 — Guitar Bains to Milkman Dead

source.excerpt: Too much tail. All that jewelry weighs it down. Like vanity. Can't nobody fly with all that shit.
trail: The passage is a set piece of the novel: the two men watch a white peacock in a car lot, and Guitar reads the bird as a lesson about what Milkman is carrying. Standard study guides index it to chapter 8 and to Guitar as the speaker the flight motif ↗.

The Buddha attribution has no textual home. Bodhipaksa’s Fake Buddha Quotes traces the meme back to Morrison — to page 179, in the edition it cites — and notes that whoever converted it into scripture had the sense to drop the profanity: ‘a dead giveaway,’ in his words the debunk ↗. No translation of the Pali canon reads like that.
A second wording from the same speech — ‘Wanna fly, you got to give up the shit that weighs you down’ — circulates widely and is also Morrison’s. Both are the novel; neither is a proverb.
source.excerptNote: The published wording, quoted briefly for identification and commentary. We keep the swear word because it is the evidence: it is the single thing the fake version had to remove.

source.rightsNote: In copyright — and the misattribution is what obscures that. Song of Solomon was published in 1977 and Toni Morrison died in 2019; the novel is protected in the United States into the 2070s and, on a life-plus-seventy term, until 2089 in the UK and EU. A short quotation with author and title is ordinary practice. Selling it on a print, a candle or a yoga-studio wall is not, and calling it a Buddha quote does not make it free — it just makes a living estate’s property look like a 2,500-year-old public-domain teaching. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Toni Morrison
author.heading: About Toni Morrison
author.metaLine: 1931–2019 · American novelist, editor, and Nobel laureate
author.bio: Toni Morrison spent years as an editor at Random House before her own novels — Song of Solomon, Beloved, Sula — made her the first Black woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Her people talk like people: profane, funny, mid-argument. That is precisely why her lines get laundered on the way to the internet, arriving smooth, solemn and stripped of the character who said them and the reason he was saying it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one is a laundering operation, and you can see the seams. A named living-memory novelist becomes an anonymous ancient sage, a peacock in a car lot becomes a metaphysical principle, and a swear word disappears.

items.why: Nothing resembling it appears in the Pali canon or any recognised Buddhist scripture, and no sutta number is ever offered with the meme — because there is none to offer. Fake Buddha Quotes traces the line to Morrison and flags the dropped profanity as the giveaway the debunk ↗.

Morrison’s line ends ‘Can’t nobody fly with all that shit.’ The inspirational version replaces that with ‘everything that weighs you down’ — which is a paraphrase of the meaning and a deletion of the voice.

Guitar Bains says it to Milkman, about a peacock, in a novel where flight is also abandonment — men who fly away leave women and children behind. Morrison is not handing out life advice; she is setting a trap.

An unattributed sage costs nothing and asks no permission. A Nobel laureate who died in 2019 has an estate. The false credit is not just sloppy — it is commercially useful to whoever is printing the mug.

misattribution.truthLine: Toni Morrison, Song of Solomon (1977) — spoken by Guitar Bains about a peacock, profanity included the scene ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The image does the work: a peacock, the most spectacular bird available, grounded by its own splendour. Everyone recognises the feeling of being weighed down by things they chose and now cannot put down.

Morrison also gets there in one breath and no abstractions — tail, jewellery, vanity, done. That compression is why it survives the trip through the internet, even when everything around it is thrown away.
detailsBody: The profanity is not decoration. It is Guitar’s voice, and the whole point is that this wisdom arrives from a young Black man in a car lot rather than from a temple.
In the novel, flight is not straightforwardly good. Men fly away; the people they leave behind are the cost. The meme keeps only the uplift.
It is being said to Milkman about Milkman — an accusation about his life, not a slogan for yours.
The Buddha credit strips the swear, the peacock, the speaker and the copyright in a single move. Fixing the attribution puts all four back.
context.pull: The swear word is the evidence. It is the one thing the fake version had to remove.
